literal: Yang's brothers led one another in building huts beside the tomb, carrying earth to form the grave mound.
idiomatic: His brothers camped together by the grave and piled earth into a mound.

literal: What the court admired in Yang was issued in an edict of praise; his residential lane was renamed Filial-End Lane.
idiomatic: The court commended him by edict and renamed his neighborhood Filial-End Lane.

literal: When mourning ended he was due to inherit; he could not bear to succeed as marquis.
idiomatic: When mourning ended he should have taken the marquisate, but he refused.

literal: The envoy in the end never accepted it.
idiomatic: He never did accept the title.

literal: In early Qi Tianbao the Prince of Changshan recommended Yang's ability; Wensuan personally appointed him Attendant of the Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: In early Tianbao the Prince of Changshan recommended Yang, and Emperor Wensuan personally made him Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.

literal: He was transferred to Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
idiomatic: He was promoted to director in the Ministry of Personnel.

literal: Sizong, Prince of Shangluo, was Qingdu Intendant; Yang was recruited as chief of the district and drew salary as a Beiqiu county officer.
idiomatic: When Sizong of Shangluo served as Qingdu intendant, he made Yang district chief with a stipend from Beiqiu.

literal: He suffered his mother's death; grief and longing wasted him, nearly unable to bear mourning; it reached grave illness, prostrate on bed and pillow, and he also developed wind ailment.
idiomatic: After his mother died he grieved until he nearly collapsed; he lay bedridden and developed a wind disorder.

literal: His fifth younger brother Bo fell ill; at the end he told his brothers: "Elder brother is so frail and ill, by nature utterly loving; on the day of Bo's death you must not let elder brother know; sounds of weeping must not be heard penetrating, lest it move him."
idiomatic: His fifth brother Bo, dying, told the family: "Our eldest is frail and tender-hearted—when I die he must not hear it; no weeping must reach him or it will break him."

literal: " The family only at the ancestral procession told him.
idiomatic: The family told him only when the funeral cortege set out.

literal: When Yang heard it he grieved in anguish; one sob and he expired.
idiomatic: Yang heard and sobbed once—and died.

literal: Age forty-eight.
idiomatic: He was forty-eight.

literal: Yang from his time in court ranks was earnest, cautious, and thorough.
idiomatic: In office Yang was earnest, careful, and meticulous.

literal: He did not speak of others' faults, did not boast of his own strengths; discourse was clear and far-reaching; he had judgment of human relations; court and countryside deeply mourned him.
idiomatic: He never gossiped about faults or trumpeted his gifts; his speech was measured and discerning, and all who knew him grieved.

literal: Posthumously awarded General of the Guards and Governor of Qingzhou; posthumous title Wen.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made General of the Guards and Governor of Qingzhou, with the posthumous name Wen.

literal: Writings in fourteen scrolls circulated in the world.
idiomatic: Fourteen scrolls of his writings circulated.

literal: Many of Qi's suburban and temple songs were composed by Yang.
idiomatic: Many of Northern Qi's temple and suburban hymns were Yang's work.

literal: His son Yi, styled Dan, inherited the marquisate of Shiping.
idiomatic: His son Yi, styled Dan, took the marquisate of Shiping.

literal: Yi was clever, keen, broadly learned, with literary talent; at nineteen he was nominated Qi prefectural outstanding talent.
idiomatic: Clever and widely read, Yi showed literary talent and at nineteen was nominated prefectural outstanding talent.

literal: He passed through Secretariat Gentleman, Literary Scholar to the Prince of Nanyang, and Regular Attendant of the Unimpeded Cavalry; he awaited orders at the Wulin Hall and concurrently served as Regular Cavalry Attendant.
idiomatic: He served as secretariat gentleman, literary scholar to the Prince of Nanyang, and regular attendant of the unimpeded cavalry, awaiting orders at the Wulin Hall.

literal: Receiving the Chen envoy, on return he was concurrently Secretariat Drafter and added Regular Attendant of the Unimpeded Cavalry.
idiomatic: After receiving a Chen envoy he was also made secretariat drafter and regular attendant of the unimpeded cavalry.

literal: Yi was most expert in the Five Classics; in the hall they called him the Stone Classics.
idiomatic: Yi knew the Five Classics best; colleagues called him the living Stone Classics.

literal: People made a saying: "The Five Classics have no match—there is Lu Yi."
idiomatic: A saying ran: "No one matches him on the Five Classics—there is Lu Yi."

literal: Yang's second younger brother Jun, styled Yunxiang.
idiomatic: Yang's second brother Jun, styled Yunxiang.

literal: From Secretariat Drafter he passed through Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate and Regular Attendant; he died as Governor of Eastern Guangzhou.
idiomatic: He rose from secretariat drafter through the yellow gate to regular attendant and died as governor of Eastern Guangzhou.

literal: Jun's younger brother Yao, styled Yunmai, also passed through Secretariat Drafter and Regular Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate; provisionally Equal in Rank to the Three Dukes and Governor of Qinzhou.
idiomatic: Jun's brother Yao, styled Yunmai, held the same court posts and served provisionally as equal to the three dukes and governor of Qinzhou.

literal: In Wuping he was besieged by raiders.
idiomatic: During Wuping raiders besieged his city.

literal: After more than a hundred days he was promoted to Grand Guardian Equal in Rank to the Three Dukes.
idiomatic: After a hundred-odd days he was made grand guardian equal to the three dukes.

literal: In the city plague was rife; more than half died; the people had no divided hearts.
idiomatic: Plague killed more than half the city, yet morale never cracked.

literal: He fell ill and died.
idiomatic: He died of illness.

literal: When the city fell, the Chen general Wu Mingche, because Yao had good government and officials and people cherished him, reported to the Chen ruler and returned his corpse; family and accumulated goods were not violated.
idiomatic: When the city fell, Wu Mingche of Chen, honoring Yao's good rule, had his body returned unharmed and forbade looting.

literal: Posthumously awarded Grand Guardian Equal in Rank to the Three Dukes and Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made grand guardian equal to the three dukes and vice minister of the masters of writing.

literal: His son Xuanqing held the post of Gentleman of the Masters of Writing for Provisions.
idiomatic: His son Xuanqing was gentleman of the masters of writing for provisions.

literal: Yao's younger brother Qian, styled Yunyi, also passed through Secretariat Drafter and Regular Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: Yao's brother Qian, styled Yunyi, also served as secretariat drafter and regular gentleman of the yellow gate.

literal: At the end of Wuping he was Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
idiomatic: At the end of Wuping he directed the ministry of personnel.

literal: Qian's younger brother Bo, styled Yunzheng, loved learning and had conduct and restraint; he died as Assistant in the Bureau of Writings.
idiomatic: Qian's brother Bo, styled Yunzheng, was studious and upright and died as assistant in the bureau of writings.

literal: Bo's younger brother Yan Shi, styled Yunfang, was known in youth for conduct and restraint.
idiomatic: Bo's brother Yan Shi, styled Yunfang, was known young for integrity.

literal: When grown he loved learning and understood regulated prose.
idiomatic: As an adult he studied hard and wrote well.

literal: Yuan Xu, Prince of Xiangcheng of Wei, brought him in as military aide; he left office on his father's mourning.
idiomatic: The Prince of Xiangcheng Yuan Xu took him as aide; he left office when his father died.

literal: Grief and ruin nearly unbearable for mourning; with his brother Yang he built huts at the tomb.
idiomatic: Grief nearly destroyed him; he camped at the tomb with his brother Yang.

literal: The villagers esteemed them and all came to the tomb side to inquire after them;
idiomatic: Neighbors honored them and flocked to the graveside to console them;

literal: at new and full moon, carriages and horses were unceasing.
idiomatic: on every new and full moon the road was never empty of visitors.

literal: Chief Secretariat Xing Shao of Hejian memorialized to recommend him.
idiomatic: Chief Secretariat Xing Shao of Hejian recommended him by memorial.

literal: Before a reply, the Prince of Pengcheng You as Governor of Sizhou summoned him to supplement as chief clerk.
idiomatic: Before the court answered, You, Prince of Pengcheng and governor of Sizhou, made him chief clerk.

literal: Later he passed through Eastern Attendant of the Inner and Outer Offices.
idiomatic: He later served as eastern attendant in the inner and outer offices.

literal: His elder brother Yang was due to inherit their father's marquisate of Shiping; because Yan Shi was youngest among the brothers he memorialized to yield the fief to him; Yan Shi firmly declined and it stopped.
idiomatic: Elder brother Yang was to inherit Shiping; he tried to yield to the youngest, Yan Shi, who refused and the matter ended.

literal: The age praised friendship, fraternal duty, and filial righteousness gathered in one clan.
idiomatic: The age praised their fraternal bond and filial piety as unrivaled in one house.

literal: He was Secretariat Drafter and Regular Attendant of the Unimpeded Cavalry.
idiomatic: He became secretariat drafter and regular attendant of the unimpeded cavalry.

literal: Whenever Chen envoys arrived, the chief guest was always chosen with care; those Yan Shi received numbered six parties in all.
idiomatic: Whenever Chen envoys came, the court picked its best host—Yan Shi entertained six missions in succession.

literal: He passed through Secretariat and Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: He served in the secretariat and as gentleman of the yellow gate.

literal: Later because he would not flatter eunuchs he met slander and was sent out as Governor of Zhongshan; he had benevolent government.
idiomatic: Later, refusing to court eunuchs, he was slandered out to Zhongshan, where he ruled with kindness.

literal: Several years later he was summoned as Director of the Ministry of Personnel and Regular Attendant; he was also appointed Grand Master of Splendid Glory with Silver Seal and Blue Ribbon, provisionally Equal in Rank to the Three Dukes, acting Governor of Zhengzhou; soon removed as Attendant of the Gentlemen of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: Years later he returned as personnel director and regular attendant, then silver-seal grand master acting equal to the three dukes and governor of Zhengzhou, soon gentleman of the yellow gate.

literal: At the end of Wuping the imperial carriage went to Jinyang; the Prince of Northern Ping garrisoned Ye; Yan Shi was entrusted with capital secrets, known for weighty caution.
idiomatic: When the emperor went to Jinyang and the Prince of Northern Ping held Ye, Yan Shi was left with capital secrets, trusted for his caution.

literal: When Emperor Wu of Zhou pacified Qi he appointed Yan Shi junior grand master and transferred him to junior admonisher; he was enfeoffed as Baron of Linshui.
idiomatic: After Zhou's conquest of Qi he made Yan Shi junior grand master and junior admonisher, baron of Linshui.

literal: When Emperor Wen of Sui was chancellor, Yan Shi fell ill and asked leave to return to Ye.
idiomatic: When Wen of Sui was still chancellor, Yan Shi fell ill and went home to Ye.

literal: Yu Chi Jiong was about to rebel; Yan Shi knew it and secretly took wife and children back to Chang'an.
idiomatic: Learning that Yu Chi Jiong would rebel, he slipped his family back to Chang'an.

literal: Emperor Wen praised this and appointed him junior grand master of the Palace Secretariat and awarded Upper Equal in Rank.
idiomatic: Wen praised him, made him junior grand master of the palace secretariat, and gave him upper equal rank.

literal: When the emperor received the abdication he was appointed Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing on the left and advanced in rank to viscount.
idiomatic: At the founding of Sui he became left vice minister of the masters of writing and was raised to viscount.

literal: Yan Shi had long been often ill; before long, duties being heavy his illness stirred; he begged to be relieved of office; an edict allowed him to keep his rank at home.
idiomatic: Chronically ill, he soon asked to quit when heavy duties worsened his health; the throne let him keep rank at home.

literal: After more than a year he was transferred to Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
idiomatic: A year later he became vice director of personnel.

literal: Sui inherited Zhou's system; offices had no pure or base distinction; Yan Shi in office, for all he appointed, quite distinguished gentry from commoners; commentators praised this.
idiomatic: Sui kept Zhou's offices without "pure" versus "base" ranks; Yan Shi still distinguished gentry from commoners in appointments, to general praise.

literal: Later again because of illness he went out as Governor of Fenzhou and died in office.
idiomatic: Ill again, he went out as governor of Fenzhou and died there.

literal: Rui, styled Sibi, in his teens inherited the rank General Who Pacifies the Army and Prince of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: Rui, styled Sibi, inherited at barely ten as General Who Pacifies the Army and Prince of Pingyuan.

literal: Deeply refined, he loved learning and bent his will to honor scholars.
idiomatic: Refined and bookish, he humbled himself before scholars.

literal: Before twenty, people of the time already promised him the highest ministry.
idiomatic: Before twenty contemporaries already called him a future chief minister.

literal: He married the daughter of Cui Jian, Governor of Eastern Xuzhou of Boling.
idiomatic: He married Cui Jian of Boling, governor of Eastern Xuzhou.

literal: At the time Xiaowen had not yet changed northern surnames; Jian told those close: "The Prince of Pingyuan's talent and measure are not bad, but I regret his name is quite redundantly repeated."
idiomatic: Xiaowen had not yet sinicized names; Jian said to friends, "The prince has talent, but that name of his is painfully repetitive."

literal: " On Rui's marriage, returning from Eastern Xu through Ye, he met Li Biao and deeply respected and delighted in him.
idiomatic: On his wedding journey home through Ye he met Li Biao and took an immediate liking to him.

literal: He then went with him to the capital and made him a hall guest.
idiomatic: He brought Biao to the capital as a household guest.

literal: Later he was commander of the northern expedition, struck the Rouran, and greatly defeated them.
idiomatic: Later, as northern expedition commander, he routed the Rouran.

literal: He was transferred to Palace Attendant and Master of Writing for All Offices.
idiomatic: He became palace attendant and master of writing for all offices.

literal: At the time the Rouran again violated the frontier; an edict ordered Rui to attack; pursuing to Shiji, he captured their chieftain Chi'atou and several hundred men.
idiomatic: When the Rouran raided again, Rui pursued them to Shiji and took their chief Chi'atou and hundreds of captives.

literal: On return he was added Regular Attendant and transferred to Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing on the Left, heading the Northern Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: Returning, he was made regular attendant and left vice minister, heading the northern masters of writing.

literal: In the sixteenth year the five-rank noble ranks were lowered; because Li's merit shone in the former dynasty, Rui was enfeoffed Duke of Julu commandery.
idiomatic: In year sixteen ranks were trimmed; for Li's old merit Rui was made Duke of Julu.

literal: Soon he was Bearer of the Staff, Grand General Who Pacifies the North, Master of Writing, and General of the Guards; he campaigned against the Rouran, greatly defeated them, and returned.
idiomatic: Soon, staff-bearing grand general who pacifies the north, master of writing, and guards general, he smashed the Rouran again.

literal: He resigned on his mother's mourning.
idiomatic: He left office for his mother's mourning.

literal: Xiaowen was about to undertake a southern campaign; with his former rank he was recalled and appointed General Who Pacifies the South.
idiomatic: When Xiaowen planned a southern war he was recalled as General Who Pacifies the South.

literal: Rui firmly declined, asking to complete the mourning rites; an edict ordered the offices earnestly to instruct him and would not allow it.
idiomatic: Rui refused, pleading to finish mourning; the throne ordered him back and would not hear of it.

literal: He was again removed as Bearer of the Staff and Area Commander of Hengzhou, acting Master of Writing.
idiomatic: He was again made staff-bearer and area commander of Hengzhou, acting master of writing.

literal: At the time the imperial carriage was on southern campaign; he memorialized to remonstrate; the emperor did not heed.
idiomatic: While the emperor marched south he memorialized in protest; the emperor ignored him.

literal: Rui again memorialized asking the imperial carriage to return to Dai and personally attend Grand Tutor Feng Xi's funeral; he was punished by stripping Area Commander of the Three Provinces and all military affairs.
idiomatic: He asked the emperor to return for Feng Xi's funeral and lost command of three provinces' armies.

literal: Soon his title was advanced to Grand General Who Pacifies the North.
idiomatic: Soon he was promoted to grand general who pacifies the north.

literal: Because he had a memorial favoring transfer of the capital, his fief was increased by four hundred households.
idiomatic: A memorial favoring the capital move won him four hundred added households.

literal: At the time Mu Tai was Governor of Dingzhou; because of illness he asked to serve at Hengzhou; Rui was then made Governor of Dingzhou.
idiomatic: Mu Tai of Dingzhou, ill, asked to swap to Hengzhou; Rui replaced him at Ding.

literal: Before he set out, he then with Tai and others alike plotted rebellion; he was granted death in prison.
idiomatic: Before he marched he plotted with Mu Tai and others; he was ordered to die in prison.

literal: His wife and children were spared collective execution and were relocated to Liaodong.
idiomatic: His family was spared the clan penalty and exiled to Liaodong.

literal: Rui's eldest son Xidao, styled Hongdu.
idiomatic: Rui's eldest son Xidao, styled Hongdu.

literal: He had bearing and grace, a fine beard; he ranged through the classics and histories and had quite literary polish.
idiomatic: Handsome, bearded, well read, he wrote with some elegance.

literal: At first appointed Palace Scribe; transferred to Unimpeded Gentleman.
idiomatic: He began as palace scribe and became unimpeded gentleman.

literal: Because of his father's affair he was relocated to Liaodong.
idiomatic: Because of his father's crime he was exiled to Liaodong.

literal: Later he was able to return; following campaigns he offered his effort; for military merit he was enfeoffed Baron of Huaiyang and appointed Remonstrating Grand Master.
idiomatic: Later restored, he earned merit on campaign and was made baron of Huaiyang and remonstrating grand master.

literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Forward General and Governor of Yingzhou.
idiomatic: He rose to forward general and governor of Yingzhou.

literal: Xidao was skilled at controlling the frontier and had great martial strategy.
idiomatic: Xidao governed the frontier well and was a formidable strategist.

literal: He was transferred to General Who Pacifies the West and Governor of Jingzhou.
idiomatic: He became general who pacifies the west and governor of Jingzhou.

literal: He died in office; posthumously awarded General Who Pacifies the Army and Governor of Dingzhou.
idiomatic: He died in office and was posthumously made general who pacifies the army and governor of Dingzhou.

literal: Xidao had six sons: Shimao, styled Yuanwei.
idiomatic: Xidao had six sons; the eldest was Shimao, styled Yuanwei.

literal: In Tianping, because his great-grandfather Li had merit in supporting and establishing the ruler, an edict specially restored the Duke of Julu commandery and ordered Shimao to inherit.
idiomatic: In Tianping, for great-grandfather Li's role enthroning the emperor, Shimao was restored to the Julu dukedom.

literal: He held the post of Governor of Yingzhou.
idiomatic: He was governor of Yingzhou.

literal: Shimao's younger brother Shizong, styled Zhongyan, was Gentleman of the Masters of Writing for Outer Troops on the Left.
idiomatic: Shimao's brother Shizong, styled Zhongyan, was left gentleman of the masters of writing for outer troops.

literal: Shizong's younger brother Shishu, styled Youwen, was Gentleman of the Masters of Writing for Seals and Credentials.
idiomatic: Shizong's brother Shishu, styled Youwen, was gentleman for seals and credentials.
